blocks.html: Notes
There are four major components of the immune system involved in fighting off pathogens (bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites):

• 1. Antibodies and the cells that make them
  • 2. Complement
  • 3. T cells
  • 4. Non-specific effector cells
Body Temperature

• Thermal compartments: core = internal organs and muscles; shell = skin and subcutaneous fat
  • Fluctuations of temperature in the peripheral regions help maintain the core body temperature
  • Normal oral temperature = 37°C (35.5-37.7°C) – no single temperature can be used as the upper limit of normal
  • Physiological variations: circadian rhythm (peak temperature = 2 PM; lowest temperature = 4 AM), menstrual cycle, post- menopausal hot flashes and fever
  • The homeostatic control of body temperature (regulated variable) involves a negative feedback system composed of sensors, an integrating center, and effectors Thermoreceptors: sensor neurons that are activated by warmth or cold – skin, spinal cord, abdominal viscera, brain
  • Hypothalamus integrates the input from thermoreceptors – anterior = heat (front, fire), posterior = cold (back, brrr)
  • Feedforward mechanism: the body acts in anticipation of thermal changes
  • 1°C increase in body temperature = 4.4 bpm increase in HR
  • Thermoregulation reaches adult levels once puberty ends – girls = 13-14 years; boys = 17-18 years

blocks.html: Innate Immunity

• Clotting factors activate the cleavage of complement molecules into reactive subunits that have effects on local innate cells and the vasculature (initially restricted)
  • Local mast cells and tissue macrophages can recognize certain types of molecules by their molecular pattern Pattern recognition receptors (PRR) – toll-like receptors (TLR)
  • Pathogen associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) – recognize bacterial lipopolysaccharide, CpG motifs
  • Damage associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) – recognize molecules released in response to tissue damage
  • The activation of mast cells causes the secretion of histamine, resulting in increased permeability (tumor, dolor) and vasodilation (rubor, calor)
  • Blood flows into the area of the injury
  • Plasma containing antibodies and compliment flows out of the blood and into the tissue
  • The activation of macrophages leads to the secretion of cytokines and chemokines and attraction of other leukocytes to the site
  • Cytokines influence the expression of adhesion molecules on the surface of vascular endothelial cells
  • Important cytokines: TNF, IL-1 Important chemokines: IL-8, C3a
  • Neutrophils, T cells, and more macrophages come flooding into the site of inflammation
  • Local dendritic cells that have been stimulated to be phagocytic by the inflammatory response take up the digested bacterial material and travel to the local draining lymph node, where they present antigen to T cells and provide antigen for B cell uptake
Antibodies and the Cells that Make Them
• Antibodies/immunoglobulins recognize specific antigen and bind to pathogens to bring them to the attention of other parts of the immune system (complement, phagocytic cells)

• Antibody is made up of four polypeptide chains held together by disulphide bonds
  • 2 identical heavy chains – μ, δ, γ, α, ε
  • 2 identical light chains – kappa, lambda
  • Fab region = N-terminal ends of the light chain + N-terminal ends of the heavy chain → antigen binding region
  • Consists of a hypervariable area that is encoded by gene elements that undergo random gene rearrangement 5’ to 3’: 300-1000 variable heavy (VH), 13 diversity heavy (DH; heavy only),
  • 4 joining heavy (JH), constant (C) regions
  • During development of young B cells, they undergo immunoglobulin gene rearrangement, where splicing, deletion, and recombination occurs to make one gene sequence Great structural diversity to recognize any and every antigen the body encounters
  • Fc region = C-terminal ends of the heavy chain → biological activity of the antibody Binds to receptors on phagocytic cells to induce phagocytosis
  • Binds to Fc receptors on mast cells before the antibody reacts with antigen
  • Binds to complement to initiate the complement activation pathway

blocks.html: Pre-B cell to B cell

• For a B cell to be functional, it needs to have a functional antibody on its surface
  • B cells develop from stem cells in the bone marrow
  • Pre-B cells rearrange the gene for antibody heavy chains, attach to surrogate light chains, and are brought to the cell surface
  • Heavy chain passes the test if the composite molecule on the surface activates Bruton’s tyrosine kinase (BTK) – allelic exclusion
  • Failure to activate BTK will lead to pre-B cell death – gets a second chance with the second allele
  • Successful light chain gene rearrangement leads to the expression of fully developed IgM and IgD on the surface of the B cell, which marks the transition from pre-B cell to a mature naïve B cell
Naïve B cell = has not seen an antigen yet

• New naïve B cells enter the circulation and travel through the blood to lymphoid organs
  • Each naïve B cell has a different antibody on its surface; each individual B cell has hundreds of thousands of antibodies on its surface that are identical and all bind to the same site on the recognized antigen
  • Once a B cell makes surface IgM, it can then make a different class of antibody (class switch), which involves a change in the Fc region of the antibody, NOT in the Fab region – changes the class and function of the antibody, but not its antigen specificity
  • In the lymph nodes, naïve B cells may encounter an antigen recognized by their surface antibodies
  • Many (more than 99%) naïve B cells circulate their entire life span without encountering antigen, and die within a few days
B cell activation

• B cells can recognize antigen in its native form as soluble protein, unlike T cells which require antigen to be degraded and presented on the surface of an antigen presenting cell in the context of MHC
  • If the B cell comes in contact with the antigen, the B cell becomes activated
  • After the antigen binds to the surface antibody on the B cells, receptor-mediated endocytosis takes place
  • The antibody and antigen are internalized by the B cell in an endocytic vesicle
  • Digestive enzymes break the antigen down into individual peptides
  • Free peptides bind to MHC in the open grooves of the MHC II molecule on the vesicle membrane
T and B cell interaction

• 1. B cells present antigen plus MHC II to an activated CD4+ T helper (Th) cell specific for that antigen
  • 2. The B and T cells form a conjugate, and cytokines are produced and released by T cells
  • 3. Cytokine induced signals (IL-4) in the B cell stimulate proliferation and differentiation
B cell differentiation into plasma cells

• B cells are small lymphocytes and have a thin rim of cytoplasm around the nucleus
  • Plasma cells are much larger and contain abundant endoplasmic reticulum and cytoplasm – produce and secrete antibody
  • Many B cells differentiate into plasma cells, a few differentiate into B memory cells, and some daughter cells continue to divide
Antibody secretion

• Plasma cells are the final stage of development of B cells which have recognized antigen, been stimulated by helper T cell- derived cytokines, and secrete the antibodies found in the circulation
  • Primary response (IgM, some IgG): the first time antigen is seen – blood level of antibodies takes a few days to increase
  • Secondary response (IgG): persistence of the antigen or re-exposure to the same antigen is much faster and more robust
Memory B cells

• The secondary response is dependent on long-lived memory B cells
  • Generated in lymphoid tissue after B cell activation and proliferation; reside in BM, lymph nodes, mucosal sites, and spleen
  • Express high affinity surface antibodies which enable them to be activated by lower levels of antigen than naïve B cells
Antigens and antigen-antibody interaction

• Antigen: a substance capable of inducing a specific immune response – generate an antibody response
  • Usually foreign proteins that enter the body via an infection, but sometimes the body’s own proteins are treated like antigens
  • The pathogen itself is not an antigen – the proteins and carbohydrates that make up the protein are antigens
  • A pathogen could have thousands of molecules that would be recognized as antigens by the immune system – epitopes
  • Antigens are recognized by the immune system by B cells (surface antibody) and T cells (T cell receptor)
  • Antibodies can recognize antigen on the surface of bacteria or viruses, as well as antigen free-floating in the tissues
Complement

• The complement cascade consists of a series of protein proenzymes present in the blood that are converted to active enzymes by interaction with pathogens and with each other
  • It resembles the coagulation pathway, and coagulation often results in the complement cascade being activated
Two major ways of activating the complement cascade:

• 1. Classical pathway: C1, C4, and C2 are activated by the Fc regions of IgG or IgM after the antibody has bound to antigen
  • 2. Alternate pathway: Factor B, D, and P (properdin) are directly activated by certain pathogens
  • The classical and alternate pathways converge on C3 (split into C3a and C3b)
  • C3a = activates mast cells to release mediators which cause local vascular permeability and vasodilation; chemotactic factor for phagocytic immune cells C3b = binds directly to the surface of foreign organisms/immune complexes and tags them for destruction by
  • phagocytes; reacts directly with other components of the complement cascade (C5-9) to produce the MAC attack
There are four major outcomes of activating this cascade:

• 1. Local vasodilation and increased vascular permeability – C3a, C4a, C5a = anaphylatoxins Binding of anaphylatoxins to their receptors on mast cells and basophils induces the cell to degranulate,
  • releasing mediators like histamine
  • Smooth muscle dilation on the arteriolar side in the vasculature → more blood flow to local capillaries
  • Increased permeability of endothelial lining of the blood vessels → more fluid, IgG, and complement
  • 2. Attraction of immune cells, especially phagocytes – C3a, C5a, chemokines Chemotaxis: the process whereby an immune cell is attracted to, and moves toward, a soluble factor
  • Chemokines: soluble protein molecules that have the effect of attracting cells to a particular site
  • Phagocytes are recruited to the tissue to ingest the invading organism, antigens, or debris from inflammation
  • Immune cells do NOT leak out of the blood because of increased vascular permeability like plasma proteins and water do – they must be attracted to the site by chemotaxis and penetrate through the endothelial lining of the vascular (transmigration)
  • 3. Opsonization of foreign organisms for phagocytosis – IgG, C3b
  • Opsonization: the process where particles/microorganisms become coated/tagged with molecules which bind to specific receptors on phagocytes
  • C3b non-specifically binds to foreign organisms/immune complexes during complement activation Phagocytes have surface receptors for C3b (CR3) – they bind, ingest, and degrade the tagged microorganisms
  • 4. Destruction of invading organisms by the membrane attack complex (MAC attack) – C5b, C6, C7, C8, C9
  • C5 is broken down into C5a and C5b after binding to C5 convertase
  • C5a diffuses away and has anaphylatoxin and chemotactic activity
  • C5b binds directly to the target organism and becomes the binding site for other complement components C5b will quickly degrade unless c6 binds to it, creating C5b6, to which C7 will then bind
  • C7 changes the conformation of the proteins so that they are able to insert into lipid membranes
  • C8 and C9 bind to the complex, creating the MAC
  • C5b678 will bind up to 16 molecules of C9 MAC looks like a tube with a pore in the center and is hydrophobic (like a straw)
  • MAC inserts into the membrane of the organism or cell and allows ion, water, and other small molecules to
  • freely pass through the pore; the organism will not be able to maintain osmotic integrity and will quickly die

• MHC proteins in humans = human leukocyte antigens (HLA)

blocks.html: T Cells

• T cells have antigen recognition molecules (T cell receptor – TcR) on the surface which are composed of α and β chains
  • 1. The α and β chains are associated with a group of 5 linked proteins, collectively referred to as CD3
  • Like antibody, the TcR has both a variable region (created by gene rearrangement) and a constant region
  • T cell receptor complex = α chain + β chain + associated CD3 proteins
  • The TcR will NOT bind to free antigen
T cell development

• For a T cell to be functional, it needs to have a functional T cell receptor on its surface that is able to recognize antigen as a peptide in the groove of self MHC, and is appropriately linked to CD3 for proper signal transduction
  • Pre-T cells arise from lymphoid stem cell precursors in the bone marrow, and travel in the bloodstream to the thymus
  • 1. The α chain of the TcR undergoes gene rearrangement; α chain is brought to the surface with a surrogate α chain and tested
  • 1. If it links properly with the signal transduction components, then the T cell goes on to rearrange β chain genes and put a mature T cell receptor on its surface – at this stage, the T cell is both CD4+ and CD8+ (double positive cell)
  • 2. The next step is to make sure the T cell can recognize self MHC – T cells interact with MHC bearing cells in the thymus
  • 2. If the TcR binds weakly to the MHC bearing cells, then the cell goes on to further development
  • 3. If the TcR does not bind to the MHC bearing cells, then it does not receive life prolonging signals and dies (most cells)
  • 4. If the TcR binds very strongly to the MHC bearing cells, indicating that the self-peptide and the self-MHC is their chosen antigen to respond to, then they will be killed
  • If the T cell passes both of these tests, it will become a mature double positive T cell; it will then lose either CD4 or CD8 to become a naïve CD4+ cell (helper T cell) or a naïve CD8+ cell (cytotoxic T cell)
Helper T cell (Th) activation

• Th cell activation is initiated by the interaction of TcR-CD3 complex with antigen-MHC II molecules on the surface of an APC
  • This interaction initiates a cascade of biochemical events in the T cell that results in growth and proliferation of the T cell Occurs primarily through an increase in IL-2 secretion by the T cell and an increase in IL-2 receptors on the T cell surface
  • IL-2 is a potent T cell growth cytokine which acts in an autocrine (self-stimulating) fashion to promote the growth, clonal proliferation, and differentiation of the T cell recently stimulated by antigen
  • All of its progeny will recognize the same T cell epitope of the original antigen, since they all have identical TcR
  • Naïve bystander T cells have no IL-2 receptors and thus cannot be involved
  • The activation is aided by the CD4 molecule on Th cells, as well as accessory molecules (CD45, CD28, CD2)
  • The APC also provides a co-stimulatory/second signal through B7 molecules (CD28:CD80/86) and cytokines (IL-1, IL-12)
  • Activated Th cells continue to become effector cells and help B cells become antibody producing plasma cells Th1: induced by IL-12, IFN-𝛄; secretes IL-2, IFN-𝛄, TNF-𝛃 → autoimmune responses, cell-mediated immunity
  • Th2: induced by IL-4; secretes IL-4, IL-5, IL-6 → promotes IgE/eosinophil responses, humoral immunity
Antigen presenting cells

• Antigen presenting cells (APC): a functionally defined group of cells which are able to take up antigens and present them to T lymphocytes in a recognizable form (in the groove of an MHC II molecule)
  • APC internalizes the antigen, processes it (breaks it down into antigenic peptides with lysozymes), and then expresses the antigen peptide on its surface
  • Dendritic cells are the most efficient and highly effective – they leave the site of infection and travel to the lymph node
  • Macrophages and B cells can present antigen to activated T cells and memory T cells
Cytotoxic T cell (Tc) activation

• The TcR on the CD8+ cell must interact with processed antigen on MHC I on the surface of an APC
  • The CD8+ must be stimulated by cytokines – IL-2 is supplied by activated Th cells in the vicinity or is self-produced by CD8+ cells
  • Like resting Th cells, resting Tc do not express IL-2 receptors; antigen stimulation increases the expression of IL-2 receptors on the cell surface, so only the cells recognizing the antigen will become activated and proliferate
  • Activated Tc cells mature into cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTL), which are involved in the recognition and direct killing of pathogen infected self-cells (not pathogens themselves)
  • 1. Conjugate formation between the CTP and the target cell
  • 2. Membrane attack on the target cell
  • Cytokines, enzymes, and perforin are released from the granules of the CTL by exocytosis
  • 3. Target cell death Granzyme is transported into the target cell and activates a cell suicide pathway which involves caspases
  • Apoptosis is induced
  • Fas ligand (FasL) is also expressed by CTL and binds to Fas on the target cell to activate the caspase pathway
Effector Cells of the Immune System

• Monocytes circulate in the blood after leaving the BM before they enter the tissue to mature into macrophages
  • Macrophages are activated in response to Th-derived cytokines (IFN) or from contact with bacteria or bacterial products
  • 1. Phagocytosis – recognize and remove unwanted particulate matter (products of inflammation, invading organisms, immune complexes, toxins, dying cells)
  • 2. Antigen presenting cells during secondary immune responses – activate memory T cells; quicker than transporting the antigen to the local draining lymph node for presentation to T cells
  • 3. Cytokine secretion – IL1, IL6, TNF
  • Natural killer (NK) cells = large granular lymphocytes (LGL) Have some surface markers in common with T cells, and are functionally similar to CTL (but do not have a TcR)
  • Unlike CTL, NK cells do not need to recognize specific antigen presented by MCH on the target cell to kill it
  • Produce large amounts of TNF-α → binds to TNF receptor on target cells and induced apoptosis
  • Neutrophils = polymorphonuclear cells (PMN)
  • Very short-lived cells (8 hours after release from BM) Attracted into the tissue by chemotactic factors – first cells to arrive at the site of inflammation
  • Active phagocytic cells in the tissues – oxygen dependent pathways (O2–, H2O2), nitrogen dependent pathways (NO),
  • independent pathways (defensins, digestive enzymes)
  • Eosinophils – phagocytic cells
  • Mast cells (in the tissues) – high affinity Fc receptors for IgE; stimulated by anaphylatoxins and crosslinking of surface IgE
  • Contain numerous granules with preformed mediators which can be released after stimulation (histamine, TNF-α) Stimulation also results in the production of prostaglandins and leukotrienes
  • Basophils (in the blood) – high affinity Fc receptors for IgE; involved in Type I hypersensitivity responses
Cytokines

• Cytokines: protein messenger molecules produced by immune system cells in order to communicate and orchestrate the attack
  • Maintain the normal growth, migration, and survival of immune cells
  • Includes chemokines, interleukins, and growth factor subfamilies
  • The same cytokine may be made by a number of different cells
  • The same cytokine may have different effects in different circumstances (pleiotropy)
  • Different cytokines may have the same activity depending on the situation (redundancy)
  • Cytokines often act together and increase the effects of one another (synergy)
  • Most cytokines have paracrine or autocrine effects

blocks.html: Microbiology Lab

• A laboratory devoted to the culturing, examination, and identification of microorganisms
  • Team: medical microbiologist, manager, coordinator, laboratory technologists, laboratory assistance
  • Sections: bacteriology, virology, mycology, parasitology, serology, molecular
  • Role: diagnosis and treatment of infectious diseases, infection control, public health
Laboratory Test Information Guide (LTIG)

• Test purpose and limitations
  • Patient selection criteria
  • Timing of specimen collection
  • Optimal specimen collection sites
  • Approved specimen collection methods
  • Specimen transport medium criteria/transport time/temperature
  • Specimen holding instructions if it cannot be transported immediately
  • Minimum acceptable volume
  • Availability of test
  • Turnaround time
  • Result reporting procedures
Rejection Criteria

• Unlabeled/mislabeled/incompletely labeled specimens
  • Quantity not sufficient for testing
  • Use of an improper transport medium
  • Use of improper swab
  • Specimen inappropriately handled (temperature, timing, storage)
  • Improper collection site for test requested
  • Specimen leakage from transport container
Phases of Testing

rows: Positive identification, patient preparation, sample collection, sample integrity
Standardization, operator competence, analysis, quality assurance

blocks.html: Specimen Collection

• Should be from the site of infection
  • Quantity sufficient for tests requested
  • Collect BEFORE antibiotics are given
  • Avoid contamination with normal flora
  • Number of specimens
  • Appropriate swabs/containers
  • Always deliver to the laboratory ASAP
  • Label specimens accurately – identifiers, clinical information

rows: Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), tracheal aspirate, nasopharyngeal swab (NPS)

blocks.html: Blood Culture

• Volume of blood collected is most critical
  • Disinfect the venipuncture site
  • Catheter-drawn blood cultures have a higher risk of contamination
  • Do not submit catheter tips for culture without an accompanying blood culture obtained by venipuncture
CNS Infection

• Meningitis, encephalitis, focal infections of brain parenchyma, CNS shunt infections, subdural empyema, epidural abscess
  • Routes of infection: hematogenous spread, direct spread from an infected site, anatomic defects in CNS structures, nerves
  • Ix: culture, molecular (viral – enterovirus, herpesvirus), Ag detection (fungal – cryptococcus)
  • Blood cultures should be obtained if meningitis is suspected
  • Inform the microbiology laboratory if unusual organisms are suspected
  • Collect 3-4 tubes of CSF by lumbar puncture and submit for bacterial culture and molecular testing
  • Collect as much sample as possible
Respiratory Infection

• Mechanisms of infection: aspiration, inhalation (aerosols, mycobacterium, TB), hematologic seeding
  • Specimen types: sputum, tracheal aspirate, blood culture, urine, serum, bronchial, pleural fluid, biopsy
  • Ix: clinical (signs and symptoms), radiographic features (consolidation), microbiology (culture, molecular, Ag detection, serology)

Skin and Soft Tissue Infections (SSTIs)

• Primary cutaneous infections: cellulitis, ecthyma, impetigo, folliculitis, furunculosis, erysipelas
  • Do not use the label “wound” alone
  • The specimen of choice is a biopsied sample of the advancing margin of the lesion
  • Do not ask the laboratory to report everything that grows
Antimicrobial Susceptibility

• Susceptibility testing: used to produce antimicrobial susceptibility profiles and detect resistance to therapeutic agents
  • Standardization: optimizes bacterial growth, optimizes conditions, maintains reproducibility
  • Breakpoint: minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) or zone diameter value used to categorize S, SDD, I, R, NS
  • Interpretive category: derived from microbiological characteristic, PK-PD parameters, and clinical outcome data

A method of multiplying microorganisms by letting them reproduce in culture medium under controlled laboratory conditions
-Growth media: liquid = broth, solid = agar plate; nutritive (general purpose), enrichment, selective, differential
-Specimen is streaked using a sterile loop onto solid media, the plate is incubated at the appropriate temperature (35°C) and
atmosphere (5% CO2), and then examined (24 hours = aerobes, 48 hours = anaerobes)
-Shape: punctiform (pinpoint), circular, filamentous, irregular, rhizoid, curled
-Elevation: flat, raised, convex, umbonate, umbilicate, growth into media
-Margin: entire (smooth), irregular, filamentous
-Identification methods: phenotypic, molecular, matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization-time of flight mass spectrometry
Antimicrobial susceptibility testing: the procedures used to produce antimicrobial susceptibility profiles and detect resistance

Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) – denature (95°C), anneal (68°C), elongate (72°C)
-Applications: 1 or 2 pathogens cause the majority of infections, no further characterization is required, no reliable/suboptimal
diagnostic methods, reliable diagnostic methods exist but are slow, quantitation of infectious agent burden
-Advantages: detect organisms that are nonviable, cannot be grown in culture, extremely difficult to grow, slow growing,
previously unknown; quantitate infectious agent burden in patient specimens

beyond identification is necessary, false negatives, no differentiation between colonization vs. infection

blocks.html: Viruses → acute and chronic infections

• Viruses: infectious, obligate intracellular parasites composed of DNA or RNA surrounded by a protein coat and/or membrane
  • Virions: mature virus particles that can be released into the extracellular environment
  • Capsid: protein shell that encases the genome, held together by non-covalent interactions; capsid + genome = nucleocapsid
  • Enveloped viruses: have an outer lipid bilayer, acquired by the budding of nucleocapsid through the host cell’s cytoplasmic membrane; glycoproteins are expressed on the surface of the envelope
  • Naked viruses: have no envelope and are often more resistant to harsh conditions
  • Virus morphology: helical, icosahedral (hollow, symmetrical, quasi-spherical), complex (non-symmetrical)
  • Virion components: polymerases, proteases, integrases topoisomerases, capping enzymes, proteins, lipids
  • The genome is the key unit that defines the virus
  • Gene products and regulatory signals for replication, assembly and packaging, regulation and timing of the replication cycle, modulation of host defenses, and spread to other cells and host is encoded in the viral genome
  • mRNA is always the (+) strand
  • DNA of equivalent polarity is also the (+) strand
  • Compliments of (+) strands are negative (–) strands
  • Virus replication cycle
  • 1. Attachment to cell receptors
  • 2. Entry – penetration into the cytoplasm
  • 3. Uncoating – genome and other contents released from nucleocapsid
  • 4. Protein synthesis – translation of viral mRNA
  • 5. Genome replication – new copies of genome
  • 6. Assembly of new virions
  • 7. Release of new virus from the cell – off to infect a new cell

blocks.html: Epidemiologic Terms

• Incubation period: the time from exposure to the causative agent until the first symptoms develop (unique for each disease)
  • Infectious period/period of communicability: the time during which an infectious agent may be transferred directly or indirectly from an infected person to another; may start/stop before, during, or after symptom onset/resolution
  • Generation time: the time duration from the onset of infectiousness in a primary case to the onset of infectiousness in a secondary case infected by the primary case
  • Basic reproductive number (R0): the average number of secondary infections produced by a typical case of an infection in a population where everyone is susceptible R0 > 1 (outbreak expected to continue; exponential growth); R0 < 1 (outbreak expected to end)
  • Effective reproductive number I: the average number of secondary cases per infectious case in a population made up of both susceptible and non-susceptible hosts R > 1 (number of cases will increase); R = 1 (disease is endemic); R < 1 (decline in the number of cases)
  • Antigenic drift: slow point mutations over time occurring in one virus; may result in epidemic
  • Antigenic shift: genetic elements in two viruses reassort to make a new virus/strain; may result in pandemic

blocks.html: Sepsis

• Sepsis: a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection
  • Can be caused by bacteria, viruses, or fungi
  • Sepsis is common, it is deadly, and it is an emergency – high morbidity and mortality rate (30-40%)
  • Loss of balance of proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory mediators → cellular injury → multiple organ dysfunction (MODS)
  • The effects of inflammation are no longer localized – they are systemic
  • All organs can be involved in sepsis due to microcirculation dysfunction in the arteriolar capillary networks Cardiovascular (low BP, high HR, myocardial dysfunction), respiratory (low O2, acute respiratory distress syndrome),
  • brain, coagulation system (thrombocytopenia, DIC), liver, kidneys, muscles, nerves
  • Septic shock: characterized by a low blood pressure that does not respond to fluids
  • Blood pressure is low because blood vessels (arterioles) vasodilate, and there is a loss of intravascular fluid into the interstitial space – add vasoconstrictive agents to artificially increase BP and prevent salt-water drowning/edema
  • Therapies that have been studied and do not work: activated protein C/heparin/antithrombin III, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, nitric oxide synthesis blockade, anti-TNF antibodies/TNF receptor blocking agent, interleukin receptor antibodies, platelet activating factor (GCSF), anti-endotoxin/LPS inhibition, vitamin C and other antioxidants, immunonutrition, hemofiltration
  • It is important to recognize sepsis clinically (low temperature or fevered, tachycardia, high RR, warm/flushed, low BP), and also try to identify the cause

• Retrovirus that infects CD4 T cells and destroys them, resulting in a progressive loss of cell mediated immunity

• Virus is still being replicated and destroys CD4 T cells

blocks.html: Anaphylaxis

• Anaphylaxis: a serious allergic reaction with a rapid onset (minutes to within 1 hour), which may cause death
  • 0.5-5% lifetime prevalence; 1% of ER visits for acute systemic allergic reactions receive the diagnosis of anaphylaxis
  • Caused by the systemic release of mast cell and basophil mediators
  • Anaphylaxis is highly likely when any one of the following three criteria is fulfilled:
  • 1. Sudden onset of an illness (minutes to several hours), with involvement of the skin, mucosal tissue, or both (generalized hives, itch/flush, swollen lips-tongue-uvula), and at least one of the following: a. Sudden respiratory symptoms and signs (shortness of breath, wheeze, cough, stridor, hypoxemia) b. Sudden reduced BP or symptoms of end-organ dysfunction (hypotonia/collapse, incontinence)
  • 2. Two or more of the following that occur suddenly after exposure to a likely allergen or other trigger for that patient: a. Sudden skin or mucosal symptoms and signs (generalized hives, itch/flush, swollen lips-tongue-uvula) b. Sudden respiratory symptoms and signs (shortness of breath, wheeze, cough, stridor, hypoxemia) c. Sudden reduced BP or symptoms of end-organ dysfunction (hypotonia/collapse, incontinence) d. Sudden gastrointestinal symptoms (crampy abdominal pain, vomiting)
  • 3. Reduced BP after exposure to a known allergen for that patient: a. Infants and children: low systolic BP (age-specific) or greater than 30% decrease in systolic BP b. Adults: systolic BP of less than 90 mm Hg or greater than 30% decrease from that person’s baseline
  • Treatment: remove the trigger, prompt administration of IM epinephrine (0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 solution, max dose = 0.3 mg), repeat epinephrine every 5-15 mins PRN, other drugs after epinephrine (O2, fluids, antihistamine, salbutamol, corticosteroids)

blocks.html: Allergy Testing

• Allergy testing plays a role in the diagnosis of Type I hypersensitivity reactions
  • The best allergy testing tool is the clinical Hx
  • Allergy testing sensitivity and specificity are different depending on what is being tested for and the type of testing done
  • Interpreting a test depends on the pre-/post-test probabilities and likelihood ratios, in the context of the clinical Hx
  • Pre-test probability: the clinical impression on the chance that the patient has a certain diagnosis Clinical experience, epidemiology, co-morbid conditions, risk factors, PEx findings
  • Likelihood ratio (LR): the likelihood that a given test result would be expected in a patient with the target disorder compared to the likelihood that that same result would be expected in a patient without the target disorder
  • Positive LR: the odds that a person who has what you are looking for has a positive test compared to a person who does not have what you are looking for but has a positive test; Sn/(1-Sp) Negative LR: the odds that a person who has what you are looking for has a negative test compared to a person who
  • does not have what you are looking for but has a negative test; (1-Sn)/Sp Calculate from sensitivity and specificity or use a nomogram
  • Cross reactivity: can occur when there is ~70% homology between antigens such that the tertiary structure is conserved Patients with food pollen syndrome to birch can get oral pruritis to almond
  • Food allergen proteins used for skin prick testing and serum IgE testing are commercially prepared Purified food protein – should contain all relevant allergens; amount of each allergen is variable with each batch
  • Recombinant extract – known allergens are made using bacteria vectors; often contains the major known allergens, but will not contain allergens that are not well known (false negative results); can be used to spike purified food protein extracts for clinically important allergens that are at low concentration
  • Environmental allergen proteins: dust mites (feces), cat/dog (dander), seasonal allergens (pollen), mold (spores)
